prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new precision tests of nature

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single part, B022, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. All eight of us arrived at the same configuration from different openings, and the reasons are largely independent: magic-wavelength trapping that removes the trade-off between atom number and perturbation, reproduction at about 10^-18 in several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), and results that are already physics, namely the gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, a many-body regime inside the clock, and limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. I keep stressing that I am not persuaded by support counts; what persuades me is that this is a clue extracted from nature by measurement, with a credit list that follows two identifiable steps, the concept and the record performance. Answering the chair's first question, I would accept either wording of the citation if it contains both the idea and the achieved precision, because the architecture is what separates this prize from the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes. My own wording therefore says 'invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to 10^-18'.
statement.case_against: The objections that I still cannot fully dismiss are four. First, lineage: a sceptic can say this is the third prize in one time-and-frequency family, and the citation must make the architectural novelty explicit. Second, the discovery content so far is consistency tests and upper limits, with no new effect seen; if the committee regards that as decisive, the clock is a tool and not a discovery. Third, credit: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom, and the ion-clock groups shaped the field, and I am working from recollection and the supplied list, not from primary priority documents. Fourth, timing: the redefinition of the second has not happened, and waiting for it would add external endorsement at the price of delay with no scientific gain.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a step change in measurement precision, lists the pending redefinition of the second as an open timing question, and discloses a mild personal link to the community through a year in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree on the first choice and I would not wait for the redefinition of the second. That decision belongs to the metrology community and the CIPM and depends on timetable and consensus among institutes, not on whether the science is established; the physics of reproduction across laboratories at 10^-18 is already established, and the prize is meant to recognise the discoveries, not the standards process. On his disclosure, I regard it as exactly the kind of remote connection that needs to be recorded and nothing more: he has no collaboration or supervisory tie to Katori or Ye, and a year in a laboratory long ago is unremarkable in a field this size. I see no step beyond disclosure being required.

responses.point: Mark Pearce, as chair, opened with IceCube (B002) and moved to B022, but states that discovery content so far is mostly upper limits and consistency tests with no new effect observed, and asks whether a second part such as B020 or B002 should share the prize.
responses.response: I accept the factual point that no new effect has been seen, and I would answer it in the citation and not by hiding it: the gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre and the many-body behaviour observed inside the clock are measured quantum and relativistic phenomena, and the citation's forward clause covers the tests. On a second part, I do not support one this year. B002 still has a single credited name for a large collaboration and its predecessor, and the source identifications are at modest significance, so I would not rescue it with a second part. B020 would bring the total to at least five names against our limit of three people, so a two-part configuration would force an arbitrary choice from Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger and Cirac. I would rather give a clean single part.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson moved from B018 to B022 but says it is an instrument and measurement achievement rather than a new state of matter or quantum phenomenon, and keeps B018 and B028 as alternatives.
responses.response: I share his discomfort about calling a clock a new phenomenon, and I stay with my position that the criterion is whether nature was made to give up a clue, not whether a new phase has been named. A clock that resolves a millimetre of gravitational redshift and an interacting-atom regime in the clock operates as a probe of physics, which a method such as dynamical mean-field theory is not in the same direct sense. I agree with his own diagnosis of B018, that a method with Metzner outside the credited trio is a hard prize to write a citation for. On B028 I remain the most sympathetic to it, but I would need the pairing mechanism to have settled before putting it in a primary configuration, and the credit would need a decision on Bistritzer.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks B022 first, resists widening the credit, and asks that the weighting between Katori's concept and the JILA 10^-18 performance be settled, while warning that the B020 names are contested.
responses.response: I agree with resisting the widening, and I think her weighting question is answered by the two-name structure itself: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and the first lattice demonstrations, Ye for taking it to the record regime with the large JILA team behind him. No lattice-clock contributor named in round one, including Lemonde, Gill and Ludlow, has been shown in the packet to have a priority claim on either of those two decisive steps, so I would not displace either name. If any member brings primary evidence of that kind, I would reconsider; otherwise I would regard a three-name version as an invitation to an arbitrary choice.

responses.point: Göran Johansson proposes a citation centred on the path from the magic-wavelength concept to 10^-18, and says that if the clock is judged a tool rather than a discovery, B020 is the more conceptually rich alternative.
responses.response: His wording is close to mine, and I would take the concept-to-performance structure as the template for the citation. On B020 as the fallback, I agree it is conceptually richer, but I now think it is the harder fallback to put into a final configuration because the five names do not reduce cleanly to three without an exclusion that the packet does not justify. I keep B020 and B028 as alternatives mainly because they differ in kind, a quantum-simulation platform and a condensed-matter surprise, not because I expect to use either this year.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on the citation text making the architectural step explicit.

Whether the weight of the evidence for Katori and Ye as the two decisive steps would survive primary-source scrutiny of priority claims by Lemonde, Gill and others, which I cannot check from the packet.
Whether the discovery content, so far limits and consistency tests, is enough for those members who prefer new phenomena.
If B022 fails to carry, whether B020 can be reduced to three defensible names or B028 settled on MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero with or without Bistritzer.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal has arisen from the first round that affects my position. My profile connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group) are in gravity and cosmology and have no link to any credited name on the shortlist. As Secretary I note Kroll's disclosed link through John Hall, and I see no need for any step beyond disclosure. Kroll's and Johansson's recusals on B014 do not touch my preferred configuration.
